A1.justification: Both are readable 13-page versions of the same DoDo-Code paper. The text, equations, five figures, two tables, and references support a complete comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v2 reports original computational experiments on codebook construction, code rates, loss ablations, and segment-correction reliability and timing in Section 5.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments, including the codebook cardinalities in Table 1, correction failures in Table 2, and timing results in Figure 5.

M1.justification: The embedding network, revised PNLL loss, greedy codebook search in Algorithm 1, and K-d-tree correction procedure in Section 4 are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain the same synthetic 4-ary sequence coverage for codebook construction and single-IDS correction, plus the binary length-10 visualization experiment in Section 5.1.

E2.justification: Figure 4 retains Cai et al. [9] and Gabrys et al. [10]. The VT-code, random-search, original-PNLL-loss, and brute-force comparators also remain in their corresponding experiments.

E3.justification: The experimental settings and metrics match, including code lengths, neighbor counts k=1 through 5, 10^8 correction attempts in Table 2, and timing over 10^5 segments in Figure 5.

E4.justification: The embedding-space visualization, greedy-search and PNLL-loss ablations, and sensitivity to the number of queried neighbors are retained without additional or revised analyses.

E5.justification: Both retain ten-run reporting, Table 1's averages with plus/minus values and maxima, and Figure 4's best-of-ten results. No statistical reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: All reported results match. Both report a 68.9% code rate at n=11, a maximum of 36,368 codewords there in Table 1, and zero failures in 10^8 trials for k=4 in Table 2. The plotted results are also unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations (1–8), the bounded-distance-decoder definitions, and the redundancy and complexity arguments are unchanged. No mathematical assumption, derivation, or proof is added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about deep-learning-based IDS code design, superior short-code rates, approximate optimality, and efficient decoding.

C2.justification: Both retain the same embedding-density interpretation, correction-approximation caveat, lack of an optimality proof, and limitations concerning mathematical characterization and codebook-search complexity at large lengths.

D1.justification: Section 5.6 retains the same random sequence generation, Python Levenshtein module, ten 1D-CNN layers, 64-dimensional embeddings, and source-code access information.

R1.justification: The same 50 references and research positioning are retained, including the relationships to combinatorial IDS codes, neural channel codes, and Levenshtein-distance embeddings.

P1.justification: v3 adds 'KL-AAGDM' to the first author affiliation and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. The body wording and section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: There are small typesetting, line-wrapping, and page-break shifts, notably across pages 1–3. Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–2 retain their content, captions, structure, and placement.

improvement.justification: The affiliation update and minor typesetting changes do not materially alter clarity, scientific support, or reproducibility. The methods, results, claims, and limitations remain unchanged, establishing no meaningful net difference in overall paper quality.
